Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to disprove conditional statements.

Content:
Suppose we wish to disprove a conditional statement of the following form:
[MATH: \forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)]

Content:
To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true.

Content:
The negation of our statement is

Content:
[MATH: ¬(∀x ∈ Z, P⇒Q)|≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, P∧¬Q.]

Content:
Therefore, to disprove the implication [MATH: P\Rightarrow Q,] it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that [MATH: P] and [MATH: \lnot Q] are both true. This value of [MATH: x] is a counterexample that disproves the original implication.

Content:
Let's see an example.

Content:
Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

Content:
> For any [MATH: a \in \mathbb{Z},] if [MATH: 2 \mid a,] then [MATH: 4 \mid a]

Content:
By denoting the predicates [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] as

Content:
- [MATH: P(a){:} \quad 2 \mid a]
- [MATH: Q(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a]

Content:
our statement can be written as
[MATH: \forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.]

Content:
We can disprove this statement by finding a counterexample. In other words, we need to find a value of [MATH: a] such that its negation is true.

Content:
The negation of our statement is

Content:
[MATH: ¬(∀a ∈ Z, P⇒Q)|≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, P∧¬Q; ≡∃a ∈ Z, (2∣a)∧(4∤a)]

Content:
So, we begin as follows:

Content:
> To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: a] such that
> [MATH: 2 \mid a
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 4 \not\mid a.]

Content:
Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: a=2] suffices.

Content:
> Let's choose [MATH: a = 2.] Then, we have that
> [MATH: 2 \mid 2
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 4 \not\mid 2.]

Content:
Finally, we state our conclusion:

Content:
> So, [MATH: a=2] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.

Content:
Now that we've figured out the details, let's write down the full argument.

our statement can be written as

For any [MATH: a \in \mathbb{Z},] if [MATH: 4 \mid a] and [MATH: 6 \mid a,] then [MATH: 24 \mid a.]

> For any [MATH: a \in \mathbb{Z},] if [MATH: 4 \mid a] and [MATH: 6 \mid a,] then [MATH: 24 \mid a.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
By denoting [MATH: P(a),] [MATH: Q(a),] and [MATH: R(a)] as

  • [MATH: P(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a]

  • [MATH: Q(a){:} \quad 6 \mid a]

  • [MATH: R(a){:} \quad 24 \mid a]

our statement can be written as [MATH: \forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \:(P \land Q) \Rightarrow R.]

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

[MATH: ¬(∀a ∈ Z, (P∧Q)⇒R)|≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬((P∧Q)⇒R); ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R); ≡∃a ∈ Z, (P∧Q)∧¬R; ≡∃a ∈ Z, P∧Q∧¬R; ≡∃a ∈ Z, (4∣a)∧(6∣a)∧(24∤a)]

So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: a] such that [MATH: 4 \mid a \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 6 \mid a \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 24 \not\mid a.]

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: a=12] suffices.

Let's choose [MATH: a =12.] Then, we have that [MATH: 4 \mid 12 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 6 \mid 12 \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 24 \not\mid 12.]

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, [MATH: a=12] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.

sections.normalized_html:
By denoting [MATH: P(a,b)] and [MATH: Q(a,b)] as

  • [MATH: P(a,b){:} \quad 3a \equiv 3b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6)]

  • [MATH: Q(a,b){:} \quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6)]

our statement can be written as [MATH: \forall a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.] We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true: [MATH: ¬(∀a, b ∈ Z, P⇒Q)|≡∃a, b ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃a, b ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃a, b ∈ Z, P∧¬Q; ≡∃a, b ∈ Z, (3a≡3b(mod6))∧(a≢b(mod6))] So, we begin as follows:

To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exist integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] such that [MATH: 3a \equiv 3b \: (\textrm{mod}\:6) \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad a \not\equiv b\: (\textrm{mod}\:6).]

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: (a,b) =(0,2)] suffices.

Let's choose [MATH: a = 0, \qquad b = 2.] Then, [MATH: 3a=0] and [MATH: 3b=6.]

To check that this is a required counterexample, we proceed as follows:

Hence, we have that [MATH: \underbrace{0}_{3a} \equiv \underbrace{6}_{3b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:6) \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \underbrace{0}_{a} \not\equiv \underbrace{2}_{b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:6).]

Finally, we state our conclusion:

So, the pair [MATH: a=0] and [MATH: b=2] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to disprove conditional statements.

Content:
Suppose we wish to disprove a conditional statement of the following form:
[MATH: \forall x \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x)]

Content:
To disprove this statement, we must show its negation is true.

Content:
The negation of our statement is

Content:
[MATH: ¬(∀x ∈ Z, P⇒Q)|≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃x ∈ Z, P∧¬Q.]

Content:
Therefore, to disprove the implication [MATH: P\Rightarrow Q,] it's sufficient to find one value of the variable such that [MATH: P] and [MATH: \lnot Q] are both true. This value of [MATH: x] is a counterexample that disproves the original implication.

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Disproving a Divisibility Statement

Content:
Suppose we wish to disprove the following statement:

Content:
> For any [MATH: a \in \mathbb{Z},] if [MATH: 2 \mid a,] then [MATH: 4 \mid a]

Content:
By denoting the predicates [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] as

Content:
- [MATH: P(a){:} \quad 2 \mid a]
- [MATH: Q(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a]

Content:
our statement can be written as
[MATH: \forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.]

Content:
We can disprove this statement by finding a counterexample. In other words, we need to find a value of [MATH: a] such that its negation is true.

Content:
The negation of our statement is

Content:
[MATH: ¬(∀a ∈ Z, P⇒Q)|≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃a ∈ Z, P∧¬Q; ≡∃a ∈ Z, (2∣a)∧(4∤a)]

Content:
So, we begin as follows:

Content:
> To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: a] such that
> [MATH: 2 \mid a
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 4 \not\mid a.]

Content:
Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: a=2] suffices.

Content:
> Let's choose [MATH: a = 2.] Then, we have that
> [MATH: 2 \mid 2
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 4 \not\mid 2.]

Content:
Finally, we state our conclusion:

Content:
> So, [MATH: a=2] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.

Content:
Now that we've figured out the details, let's write down the full argument.

---

Content:
Disprove the following statement:

Content:
> For any [MATH: a \in \mathbb{Z},] if [MATH: 2 \mid a,] then [MATH: 4 \mid a.]

Content:
Counterexample:

Content:
> To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample. In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: a] such that
> [MATH: 2 \mid a
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 4 \not\mid a.]
>
> Let's choose [MATH: a = 2.] Then, we have that
> [MATH: 2 \mid 2
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 4 \not\mid 2.]
>
> So, [MATH: a=2] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.

---

Item 4 — Example: Stating Counterexample Conditions

Example Prompt:
Consider the following false statement.

> If [MATH: 2a \equiv 2b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4),] then [MATH: a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)] for any [MATH: a,b \in \mathbb{Z}.]

A counterexample for the above statement would be a pair of integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] such that
[MATH: \bbox[3px, border: 2px solid black]{\phantom{RRR} }\, (\textrm{mod}\:4)
\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
\bbox[3px, border: 2px solid black]{\phantom{RRR} }\, (\textrm{mod}\:4).]

Find the missing expressions.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
By denoting [MATH: P(a)] and [MATH: Q(a)] as

- [MATH: P(a,b){:} \quad 2a \equiv 2b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)]
- [MATH: Q(a,b){:} \quad a \equiv b \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)]

our statement can be written as

[MATH: \forall a,b \in \mathbb{Z}, \: P \Rightarrow Q.]

Since this statement is false, its negation is true.

A counterexample is a particular case that disproves the statement. Equivalently, it's a case that proves the negation is true.

The negation of our statement is

[MATH: ¬(∀a, b ∈ Z, P⇒Q)|≡∃a, b ∈ Z, ¬(P⇒Q); ≡∃a, b ∈ Z, ¬(¬P∨Q); ≡∃a, b ∈ Z, P∧¬Q; ≡∃a, b ∈ Z, (2a≡2b(mod4))∧(a≢b(mod4)).]

Therefore, we have the following:

> A counterexample for the above statement would be a pair of integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] such that
> [MATH: \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2a \equiv 2b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:4)
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> \bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}a \not\equiv b} \: (\textrm{mod}\:4).]

---

Item 7 — Example: Disproving Divisibility Statements

Example Prompt:
Disprove the following statement:

> For any [MATH: a \in \mathbb{Z},] if [MATH: 4 \mid a] and [MATH: 6 \mid a,] then [MATH: 24 \mid a.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
By denoting [MATH: P(a),] [MATH: Q(a),] and [MATH: R(a)] as

- [MATH: P(a){:} \quad 4 \mid a]
- [MATH: Q(a){:} \quad 6 \mid a]
- [MATH: R(a){:} \quad 24 \mid a]

our statement can be written as
[MATH: \forall a \in \mathbb{Z}, \:(P \land Q) \Rightarrow R.]

We want to disprove this statement. In other words, we must show that its negation is true:

[MATH: ¬(∀a ∈ Z, (P∧Q)⇒R)|≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬((P∧Q)⇒R); ≡∃a ∈ Z, ¬(¬(P∧Q)∨R); ≡∃a ∈ Z, (P∧Q)∧¬R; ≡∃a ∈ Z, P∧Q∧¬R; ≡∃a ∈ Z, (4∣a)∧(6∣a)∧(24∤a)]

So, we begin as follows:

> To disprove a universal statement, it's sufficient to find a counterexample.
> In other words, we need to show that there exists an integer [MATH: a] such that
> [MATH: 4 \mid a
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 6 \mid a
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 24 \not\mid a.]

Finding a counterexample is sometimes a nontrivial task, but we only need one. In this case, substituting [MATH: a=12] suffices.

> Let's choose [MATH: a =12.]
> Then, we have that
> [MATH: 4 \mid 12
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 6 \mid 12
> \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad
> 24 \not\mid 12.]

Finally, we state our conclusion:

> So, [MATH: a=12] is our counterexample. Therefore, the given statement is false.
